messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur Vance was fifty-two when a chemical plant explosion leveled three city blocks, a man-made disaster that tore through the industrial district where he had built his career. He had rushed in with his notebook, but the blast wave threw him against a brick wall and filled his mouth with the choking, metallic tang of ruptured pipes. That specific taste still ambushes him. When he encounters it today in a restaurant broth, the memory of shattering glass and fleeing workers hits him with full force, replaying like a film that will not stop. The experience is so extreme that he sometimes questions whether it truly happened to him, yet when the recollection takes hold, he feels as though the flames are licking at his boots right now. This intense reliving makes his nervous system stay locked in high gear; he finds himself unable to relax even in his own study, because his body refuses to accept the catastrophe is over. Because his body stays so attuned to danger, ordinary unpredictability now feels like a prelude to catastrophe. An unexpected delivery driver or a sudden shift in traffic patterns immediately pushes his threat monitoring into overdrive, causing him to scan the room for potential weapons or dangerous objects he might have missed. When the specific taste of burning insulation hits him, or when he encounters an unpredictable situation at the market, the sudden surge of panic immediately drives him to adopt rigid maladaptive strategies. Those sensory anchors instantly escalate his threat system, and the resulting panic quickly feeds his negative appraisals; he begins to believe that if he thinks about the event, he will not be able to handle it. His constant scanning makes him feel perpetually unsafe, which in turn forces him to compulsively spend money just to numb the dread. His hyper-aroused state then heightens his sensitivity to triggers, meaning a photograph of an old cityscape now instantly alarms him. These appraisals then warp his recall; believing he is permanently damaged, his mind forces the memory to replay. The conviction that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore drives him to retreat into compulsive spending and rigid wall-sitting. These coping habits, however, have only deepened the wound. By constantly freezing or retreating into shopping sprees, he avoids processing the trauma, which leaves the memory more fragmented. His refusal to face the danger directly means his triggers remain entirely unextinguished. Because he never lets himself habituate to the sensations, a visual of his colleagues’ faces on a newsstand rack still triggers his threat response instantly, causing his hands to sweat and his posture to stiffen. This renewed threat arousal then pulls him back into memory replay, and the cycle tightens. These coping habits maintain his threat monitoring, as he remains too exhausted from his own avoidance to ever truly check if the house is safe, leaving him perpetually braced for the next disaster. This unrelenting threat monitoring feeds directly back into the memory, ensuring the film continues to play without resolution. The constant scanning confirms his darkest predictions; he starts to believe that if he thinks about the event, he will not be able to handle it. Because the memory replays with such ferocity, he concludes that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. When the recollection takes hold and he feels the flames right now, the overwhelming intensity pushes him to freeze completely when threatened. Each time he spends money to escape the fear, he confirms his own belief that he is fundamentally broken and that life has lost all meaning. Arthur Vance sits now at seventy-three in his dim study, a retired journalist whose notebooks are buried under unpaid bills and unopened mail. His study, quiet since his divorce years ago, feels less like a sanctuary and more like a fortified archive, where he once filed investigative reports for national publications. He finally scheduled an appointment after a recent photo album surfaced from his desk drawer, and the sudden visual of his colleagues’ faces sent him to the corner cabinet where he keeps his credit cards, his fingers trembling as he swiped one for a bottle of scotch. He is exhausted by the loop, the way each moment of dread feeds the next, but he hopes that talking to someone might finally break the spell. He fears that if he stops numbing himself, the memories will consume him entirely, yet he also hopes to reclaim the ability to feel something other than the heavy, flat exhaustion that has settled over his days. He just wants to sit in a sunlit room without listening for footsteps, and perhaps, after decades of running from a fire that never really ended, learn how to breathe again.
